episode.throughLine: A six-year-old child struggled through an early lesson, made a request with copied finger movements, and used growing language to ask a question during a search game.

contentProfile.contentNote: Lasting sight and hearing loss, frustration during communication, and an early lesson in which a teacher restrains the child in a chair. No injury is described; restraint is not presented as the cause of understanding.

facts.statement: During the early lesson reported March 6, Keller helped unpack Sullivan's trunk and was delighted by the doll. Sullivan spelled in her hand, pointed to the doll, and nodded. Keller looked puzzled, felt Sullivan's hand, imitated the repeated letters, and pointed to the doll herself.

sourceRefs.locator: Part III Education, March 6 letter: She helped me unpack my trunk through She imitated them very well and pointed to the doll.

facts.statement: Helen Keller was born June 27, 1880; Sullivan arrived March 3, 1887, when Keller was six. She was still six through the April learning episode.

sourceRefs.locator: Chronology entries June 27, 1880, March 3, 1887, and April 5, 1887.

facts.statement: An illness in early childhood left Keller unable to see or hear; its precise diagnosis is unknown.

Sullivan took the doll, shook her head, and tried to form the letters with Keller's fingers. Keller tried to seize the doll and grew increasingly angry; Sullivan forced her into a chair and held her until the teacher was nearly exhausted.

sourceRefs.locator: Part III Education, March 6 letter: Then I took the doll through I must do something to turn the current of her thoughts.

facts.statement: Sullivan interpreted Keller's anger as believing the doll was being taken away, rather than understanding the spelling exercise. This is the teacher's interpretation, not an independently recorded child statement.

sourceRefs.locator: Part III Education, March 6 letter: Then I took the doll, meaning to give it back through she thought I meant to take it from her.

facts.statement: After releasing Keller but withholding the doll, Sullivan brought cake, formed its letters, and patted the child's hand. Keller formed the letters rapidly and ate the cake; she then formed most of the doll word, received help with its final letter, and took the doll downstairs.

sourceRefs.locator: Part III Education, March 6 letter: I let her go through could not be induced to return to my room all day.

facts.statement: Through March 20 and April 3, Keller learned finger forms for more nouns and verbs through sustained spelling practice before the teacher reported understanding that everything had a name.

sourceRefs.locator: Part III Education, March 20 Helen has learned several nouns paragraph; April 3 BUT YOU MUSTN'T THINK paragraph and March 31/April 1 word list.

facts.statement: Sullivan's March 20 letter reports that Keller confused the cup and milk names with drinking gestures and still did not understand that everything had a name.

sourceRefs.locator: Part III, Education, Sullivan letter dated March 20, 1887, paragraph beginning Helen has learned several nouns.

facts.statement: Sullivan's April 10 letter says Keller eagerly asked for object names, wanted friends to spell, tried to teach letters to others, and replaced earlier gestures when she learned words.

sourceRefs.locator: Part III, Education, April 10 letter, opening paragraph.

facts.statement: A search game using a hidden ball or spool initially defeated Keller: she searched unsuitable places and soon gave up. With practice she sustained the search longer.

sourceRefs.locator: Part III, Education, April 24 letter, paragraphs beginning We play a little game and Again when I hid the spool.

facts.statement: The April 24 letter reports that Keller commonly expressed full requests through single words with gestures and was not yet fluent in finger language. This is not a claim about oral speech or an absolute inability to form any short sentence.

sourceRefs.locator: Part III Education, April 24, The new scheme works and Milk with a gesture paragraphs; compare Give baby candy in the later Friday anecdote.

facts.statement: On the morning recorded April 24, Sullivan hid a cracker. Keller searched unsuccessfully, ran to Sullivan, made her open her mouth very wide, and investigated it. Finding no trace of the cracker, Keller pointed to Sullivan's stomach and spelled eat. The precise room and elapsed duration are not given.

sourceRefs.locator: Part III Education, April 24: This morning I hid a cracker through she pointed to my stomach and spelled eat.

facts.statement: Sullivan interpreted Keller's pointing and spelling eat during the cracker search as asking whether the teacher had eaten it. This is the teacher's interpretation of the documented words and gestures, not a verbatim full sentence from Keller.

sourceRefs.locator: Part III Education, April 24 cracker search, final clause meaning Did you eat it?

facts.statement: By May 8 Keller adopted finger words for small and large in place of gestures. Sullivan could ask for a large book or small plate, and on the recorded morning Keller added a word for and when told to shut a door. She used small and very small for puppies, stones, her sister, and steps.

sourceRefs.locator: Part III Education, May 8: Helen is learning adjectives through and lock; later puppy comparison paragraph She noticed one of the puppies through applying the new words to all kinds of objects.

facts.statement: By May 16 the teacher and child took long morning walks; Keller asked about things along the way and returned eager to tell her mother. She still made mistakes and tangled words and phrases; Sullivan supplied missing words or sentences.

sourceRefs.locator: Part III Education, May 16: We have begun to take long walks through I supply a word here and there, sometimes a sentence.

facts.statement: Her full name was Helen Adams Keller.

sourceRefs.locator: Opening paragraph under Where Was Helen Keller Born.

facts.statement: Keller regarded herself as a writer and worked with the American Foundation for the Blind to advocate for people with disabilities.

sourceRefs.locator: Helen Keller's Political and Social Activism section; author identity and AFB advocacy paragraphs.

arc.canonicalText:
She helped the new woman unpack her luggage in the room upstairs. She was six. Inside was a doll, and she was delighted to find it. She could not see it, and she could not hear. The woman slowly made a pattern of letters in her hand. The woman pointed to the doll.

The girl felt the woman's hand and looked puzzled. The letters came again. She copied the movements well and pointed to the doll herself. Her fingers had matched the fingers she had felt. Then the woman took the doll.
arc.sourceNote: Sullivan's March 6 published letter extract supplies the upstairs unpacking and doll lesson. The editor discloses connected extracts and slight wording changes; observer actions are recorded, not invented. AFB chronology supplies age six.

arc.canonicalText:
She tried to seize the doll. The woman shook her head and tried to form the letters with the girl's fingers. The girl grew angrier. The doll had just been in her hands. Now the other person held it, and she was trying to get it back. The woman forced her into a chair and held her there.

She had copied the hand movements, but had not understood the exchange. She thought the woman meant to take the doll away from her. The woman held her until she herself was nearly exhausted. The girl was still angry in the chair.
arc.sourceNote: One bounded early lesson: attempted seizure, increasing anger, and chair restraint. The teacher's belief about the child's understanding is marked probable in w-interpretation. No invented feeling, injury, or motive; the restraint is not justified or made the cause of language learning.

arc.canonicalText:
She made the letters in her hand again, this time for a piece of cake. The woman had let her out of the chair and brought the cake upstairs. She held it towards the girl and formed its name. The girl tried to take it. The letters came again, followed by a pat on her hand. She made the movements quickly herself.

The woman gave her the cake, and she ate it in a hurry. Then the doll was held towards her with its finger word. She made the letters, leaving one unfinished. The woman supplied it and handed her the doll. She ran downstairs with it.
arc.sourceNote: The child's documented small act is making the cake letters herself in the same upstairs lesson, then the doll letters. No claim that reward proves word meaning or that obedience causes recovery.

arc.canonicalText:
Over the next weeks, her hands learned more patterns. The finger words for a cup and milk were hard to distinguish. She pointed to the cup when she made one word. For the other, she made the sign for pouring or drinking. She still did not understand that everything had a name.

Later, she asked for names and wanted other people to spell too. But new games still defeated her. The teacher hid a ball, and she looked beneath a flat board. There was no room for the ball there. When a spool was hidden, she looked in a box too small to hold it. She soon gave up searching. With practice she searched for longer. For requests, she relied on single words and gestures.
arc.sourceNote: Forward compression from early practice to March 20, April 10 and the first search games two or three days before April 24. The water episode is omitted rather than disguised. Cup/milk confusion and failed searches are real failures, not invented metaphors or merged encounters.

arc.canonicalText:
The teacher had hidden a cracker for her to find that morning. She searched everywhere she could think of, without success. Then she ran to the teacher and made her open her mouth wide. She examined the open mouth thoroughly. There was no trace of the cracker inside. Her search had brought her to the person who had hidden the food.

She pointed to the woman's stomach and spelled the word for eat. With that word and gesture, she was asking whether the teacher had eaten it. She had not found the hidden cracker. But she had a question for the other person about where it had gone. Her fingers made the word, and her pointing filled out the question. The search was still unfinished.
arc.sourceNote: One search explicitly dated This morning in Sullivan's April 24 letter: cracker hidden, unsuccessful searching, running to teacher, open-mouth inspection, pointing, and spelling. No outcome or exact room is invented. w-question is probable observer interpretation of the child's word and gesture, not a fabricated full utterance. The ordinary search replaces the recognizable water encounter.

arc.canonicalText:
In the following weeks, she gained words for differences between things. She could ask for something small or something large with the finger words. The teacher could ask her to bring a large book or a small plate. She compared the sizes of puppies, stones, her sister, and her own steps. She was learning more than names.

On their morning walks, she found things to ask about along the way. Back home, she wanted to tell her mother what they had found. She still tangled words and phrases and made many mistakes. The teacher supplied a missing word, and sometimes a whole sentence. None of the words had restored her sight or hearing. There was more for her to learn.
arc.sourceNote: Forward compression through May 8 and May 16: size words, morning walks, telling her mother, continuing mistakes, and teaching assistance. No fluent speech, cure, completed language education, or achievement list. Age six and impairment with hand spelling may remain recognizable to a familiar reader.

arc.canonicalText:
Her name was Helen Adams Keller.

She became a writer whose work helped press for the rights of people with disabilities.

Your life is not theirs. But a piece of this story may still sit beside you.

You do not have to know how it ends to keep going. You are allowed to need more time.
arc.sourceNote: Full name and plain writer/advocacy role from AFB institutional biography. Exact distance pair and bounded permission, without promises or equivalence.

dramatizationLimits: No invented actions, causes, decisions, realizations, dialogue, physical sensations, or third-party motives. All narrative sentences are source-linked historical claims; no texture is generated.
Contemporaneous records reproduced in later books are identified as such. Later memory and observer interpretation stay qualified in facts and passage source notes.
avoidRules: Do not name a person, date, city, or institution before the bridge.
Do not equate the reader's life with the subject's, offer advice, or promise an outcome.
Do not imply that personal effort removes exclusion, poverty, disability, or the need for other people's support.
Do not use a miracle or cure narrative, equate learning with becoming fully human, or imply that sight or hearing returned.
Do not treat every recorded finger form as an understood word before the water episode.
Do not merge conflicting cup-and-water and cup-and-milk accounts into one supposedly certain scene.
Do not repeat Sullivan's racist or dehumanizing descriptions of children in the teaching letters.

sources.citation: Anne Sullivan's 1887 letters to Sophia Hopkins, reproduced in The Story of My Life (1903).
